title: Pupillary Reflexes, Light Reflex and its Lesions

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: Per the book, the near reflex has three components. Which set is printed?
questions.exp: The near reflex (first of the four pupillary reflexes) has 3 parts: accommodation, convergence and miosis. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: Fill up: the ciliospinal reflex is triggered by pain in the side of the neck or trunk, producing ______.
questions.exp: Ciliospinal reflex: pain in side of neck/trunk → ipsilateral pupil dilation. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: The book lists four pupillary reflexes. Which of the following is NOT among them?
questions.exp: The four pupillary reflexes: near (3 parts), ciliospinal, psychosensory and pupillary light reflex (PLR); VOR belongs to the vestibular apparatus, not this list. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: Which statement about the light reflex procedure is FALSE per the book?
opts: It is a dark room procedure
The hand is placed between the eyes to separate visual fields
Low light causes dilation of the pupil
Bright light causes dilation of the pupil
questions.exp: Procedure: dark room; hand between eyes → separate visual fields. Normal findings: bright light → constriction (not dilation); low light → dilation. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: You test a patient's pupillary light reflex in a dark room and place your hand between his two eyes. Per the book the purpose is to:
opts: Separate the visual fields of the two eyes
Block the consensual pathway to the opposite eye
questions.exp: The hand between the eyes separates the visual fields so each eye can be illuminated and read independently. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: Match the event with the pupil response in the book's figure — 1) Light shone on the left eye 2) Illuminated (left) pupil 3) Non-illuminated (right) pupil … A) Constricts by the direct reflex B) Constricts by the consensual reflex C) Source of the stimulus
questions.exp: Left stimulus: the illuminated pupil constricts (direct reflex) and the contralateral non-illuminated pupil constricts (consensual reflex). (Book p26)

questions.sec: Pupillary reflexes and light reflex overview
questions.q: Fill up: the consensual reflex is the constriction of the ______ pupil, that is, the pupil that is not illuminated.
questions.exp: Direct reflex = constriction of the illuminated pupil; consensual reflex = constriction of the C/L (non-illuminated) pupil. (Book p26)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: In the book's PLR pathway figure, where do the afferent fibres leave the visual pathway?
opts: After relaying in the lateral geniculate body
In the retina before the optic nerve
Before reaching the LGB, exiting from the optic tract
questions.exp: Afferent (I/L) limb: light on one eye → optic nerve; PLR fibres exit from the optic tract before reaching the LGB and reach the pretectal centre. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Match the PLR pathway station with its labelled role — 1) Pretectal nucleus 2) Internuncial neuron 3) Edinger-Westphal nucleus … A) Accessory nucleus for CN III B) Centre of the reflex in the midbrain C) Relay from the centre to the EWN
questions.exp: Pretectal nucleus = centre; the internuncial (I/N) neuron relays to the B/L EWN; EWN = accessory nucleus for CN III. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Fill up: the Edinger-Westphal nucleus supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle and is the accessory nucleus of cranial nerve ______.
questions.exp: EWN (accessory nucleus for CN III) supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Which statement about the PLR pathway is FALSE per the book?
opts: ON, OC and OT are common to the PLR and the visual pathway
The PLR efferent neurons are primarily temporal
The reflex stays strictly on the illuminated side only
The short ciliary nerve carries the final efferent limb
questions.exp: The efferent limb is B/L: from the centre via I/N neurons to both EWNs, giving direct and consensual responses; ON/OC/OT are common to both pathways; efferent neurons are primarily temporal. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Which nerve–muscle pairing is the final efferent step of the PLR per the book?
opts: Long ciliary nerve to the sphincter pupillae
Short ciliary nerve to the ciliary muscle
Long ciliary nerve to the ciliary muscle
Short ciliary nerve to the sphincter pupillae
questions.exp: B/L short ciliary nerves from the B/L ciliary ganglia supply the B/L sphincter pupillae, producing constriction. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: The book splits PLR lesions into afferent and efferent types. Which is NOT an efferent pathway lesion?
questions.exp: Efferent pathway lesions: Argyll Robertson pupil, tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis; Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is an afferent pathway lesion. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Match the afferent pathway lesion with the book's label — 1) Total (absolute) afferent defect 2) Relative afferent defect 3) I/L optic tract lesion … A) Wernicke's pupil B) Absolute afferent pathway defect C) Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD)
questions.exp: Afferent pathway lesions: total/absolute → AAPO; relative → Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD); Wernicke's pupil is the optic-tract (hemianopic) pupil. (Book p27)

questions.sec: PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
questions.q: Fill up: the book's efferent pathway lesion list is Argyll Robertson pupil, ______ pupil and pharmacological mydriasis.
questions.exp: Efferent pathway lesions: Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP), tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis. (Book p27)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: Which cause does the book give for an absolute afferent pathway defect (AAPO)?
opts: Retinal detachment and end stage optic nerve disease
Complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma or end stage optic nerve disease
questions.exp: AAPO: complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma or end stage optic nerve disease. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: All of the following are listed causes of an incomplete optic nerve lesion producing RAPD EXCEPT:
opts: Retinal detachment, since the ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons
questions.exp: RAPD causes: optic neuritis, CRAO, retinal detachment (ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons); a complete optic nerve lesion (e.g. trauma) gives AAPO, not RAPD. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: A 30-year-old with left optic neuritis undergoes the swinging flashlight test. On repeated swings to the affected (fatigued) left eye the book expects:
opts: B/L constriction of both pupils on every swing
B/L dilation of pupils when the eye with the lesion is stimulated
Only the right pupil dilates on each swing
No change in either pupil with repeated swings
questions.exp: Swinging flashlight test in RAPD: on presentation B/L constricted; on stimulus B/L constrict on one eye; swinging to the other eye the pupils dilate in the meantime and constrict again; repeat (fatigue the lesioned ON) → B/L dilation when the lesion eye is stimulated. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: Which statement about the light reflex in AAPO is FALSE per the book's table?
opts: Light on the lesion side produces no constriction of either pupil
The I/L direct light reflex is absent
The C/L consensual reflex is absent
questions.exp: In AAPO light on the lesion side leaves both pupils un-constricted (I/L DLR and C/L DLR absent), yet the pupils remain always equal in size — isocoria. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: Fill up: in both AAPO and RAPD the pupils are always equal in size, a condition the book names ______.
questions.exp: Pupils relative to each other: always equal in size — isocoria — in both afferent pathway lesions; anisocoria is the efferent hallmark. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: Per the symptom row of the book's comparison table, what accompanies AAPO?
opts: I/L anopia d/t the optic nerve lesion
Loss of accommodation on near effort
No symptom is listed in the table
questions.exp: Symptom row: AAPO — I/L anopia (d/t optic nerve lesion); RAPD — none (–). (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: A 68-year-old with acute left CRAO is examined. The book notes the ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons. The expected pupillary finding is:
opts: A relative afferent defect in the right eye
A relative afferent defect in the left eye
Anisocoria with a dilated left pupil
An absolute afferent defect in the left eye
questions.exp: CRAO is an incomplete optic nerve lesion → RAPD in the affected eye; the pupils stay isocoric. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Afferent lesions — AAPO versus RAPD
questions.q: Match the finding with the lesion in the book's comparison — 1) I/L and C/L DLR absent when the lesion side is illuminated 2) Swinging flashlight test with dilation on the fatigued eye 3) Isocoric pupils in both lesions … A) Characteristic of RAPD B) Characteristic of AAPO C) Shared by AAPO and RAPD
questions.exp: The light reflex test (both DLRs absent on the lesion side) characterizes AAPO; the swinging flashlight test characterizes RAPD; isocoria is shared by both. (Book p28)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Which combination defines Wernicke's hemianopic pupil per the book?
opts: Bitemporal hemianopia with a chiasmal lesion
Central scotoma with an optic nerve lesion
I/L homonymous hemianopia with an optic tract lesion
C/L homonymous hemianopia with an I/L optic tract lesion
questions.exp: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil: site of lesion — I/L optic tract; presentation — C/L homonymous hemianopia. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Light is shone on the hemianopic (invisible) half of the field in a patient with Wernicke's pupil. Per the book the expected response is:
questions.exp: Light stimulus on the hemianopic/invisible VF → no constriction; light on the normal VF → pupil constriction. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Which statement about the Argyll Robertson pupil is FALSE per the book?
opts: It is a feature of tertiary syphilis (neurosiphilis)
The pupillary light reflex is B/L absent
questions.exp: ARP causes: neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis, may present with seizures and confusion), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; PLR B/L absent; accommodation present; NO dilation with atropine. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Fill up: the book's mnemonic for ARP, 'ARP PRA', stands for Accommodation Reflex Present and ______.
questions.exp: Mnemonic ARP PRA: Accommodation Reflex Present, Pupillary Reflex Absent. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Match the ARP lesion site with the internuncial neurons it affects — 1) Periaqueductal grey 2) Posterior commissure … A) C/L internuncial neurons B) I/L internuncial neurons
questions.exp: Periaqueductal grey affects I/L internuncial neurons; posterior commissure affects C/L internuncial neurons; lesions are usually B/L. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: Per the book, ARP lesions are usually:
questions.exp: Lesions in ARP are usually B/L. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: A 55-year-old with tertiary syphilis shows small constricted pupils that do not react to light but constrict on near effort. Per the book's postulate the presenting miosis persists because the EWN:
opts: Is directly stimulated by the spirochaete
Receives neither excitatory nor inhibitory signals
questions.exp: On presentation both pupils are constricted; postulate: the supra-nuclear pathway is destroyed through the periaqueductal area/tectum (–), so the EWN receives neither excitatory/inhibitory signals → miosis. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
questions.q: All of the following are listed causes of the Argyll Robertson pupil EXCEPT:
questions.exp: ARP causes: neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; papilledema is a cause of secondary optic atrophy, not of ARP. (Book p29)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: Match the efferent lesion with its site of lesion in the book's table — 1) Tonic/Adie's pupil 2) Pharmacological mydriasis … A) Drug action: supranuclear inhibition of the EWN B) Ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve
questions.exp: Tonic/Adie's pupil: ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve; pharmacological mydriasis: drug action — supranuclear inhibition of the EWN (e.g. atropine). (Book p30)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: All of the following are listed causes of the tonic pupil EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Tonic pupil causes: HZV ganglionitis, diabetes/alcoholism → peripheral neuropathy, trauma; Holmes-Adie pupil = tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. Horner syndrome is not in this list. (Book p30)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: Per the book, Holmes-Adie pupil is:
opts: Tonic pupil with ↓ deep tendon reflexes
questions.exp: Holmes-Adie pupil: tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. (Book p30)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: Fill up: denervation hypersensitivity of the tonic pupil is demonstrated by constriction with ______ dilute pilocarpine.
questions.exp: Denervation hypersensitivity: the denervated sphincter pupillae overexpresses receptors (mushrooming), so it hyperreacts and constricts with 0.125% dilute pilocarpine. (Book p30)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: Which statement about the tonic pupil is FALSE per the book?
opts: The I/L pupil does not constrict to light while the C/L pupil constricts
The near reflex is present with slow, vermiform dilating movements
The two pupils are equal in size
questions.exp: The tonic pupil shows anisocoria (unequal pupil size), which differentiates it from afferent pathway lesions (isocoria); I/L DLR ↓ and CLR absent, near reflex present (slow vermiform), denervation hypersensitivity to 0.125% pilocarpine. (Book p30)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: A 28-year-old's anisocoria is greater in the dark and the abnormal pupil is the smaller one. Per the book's algorithm the next test is:
questions.exp: Anisocoria greater in the dark → the lesion/abnormal pupil is the constricted one (the normal pupil can dilate in the dark, the abnormal one cannot) → 1% apraclonidine test. (Book p31)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: Match the anisocoria pattern with the book's diagnosis — 1) Greater in dark, small pupil, apraclonidine positive (abnormal pupil dilates) 2) Greater in dark, small pupil, apraclonidine negative 3) Greater in light, dilated pupil, constricts to 0.125% pilocarpine … A) Physiological anisocoria B) Horner's syndrome C) Tonic pupil
questions.exp: Small pupil with dark > light: apraclonidine positive → Horner's syndrome; negative → physiological anisocoria (anisocoria only in dark). Dilated pupil with light > dark constricting to 0.125% pilocarpine → tonic pupil. (Book p31)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: The book defines anisocoria as a difference of at least ______ in pupil size between the two eyes.
questions.exp: Anisocoria: difference ≥0.4 mm in pupil size between the two eyes. (Book p31)

questions.sec: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria algorithm
questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer's anisocoria is greater in the light; the abnormal pupil is dilated with normal shape. It does not constrict to 0.125% pilocarpine and also not to 1% pilocarpine. Per the flowchart the diagnosis is:
questions.exp: When the abnormal pupil does not constrict even with 1% pilocarpine, a weak agonist cannot reverse mydriasis by a strong antagonist like atropine → pharmacological mydriasis; a 3rd CN palsy pupil would constrict with 1%. (Book p31)

units.title: The pupillary reflexes and the light reflex overview
units.guide: Four pupillary reflexes: near (accommodation, convergence, miosis), ciliospinal (pain in side of neck/trunk → I/L pupil dilation), psychosensory (stress/emotion → dilation) and the pupillary light reflex (PLR). PLR overview: dark room procedure; hand between the eyes separates the visual fields. Normal: bright light → constriction, low light → dilation. Illuminating one eye constricts the illuminated pupil (direct reflex) and the non-illuminated C/L pupil (consensual reflex).

units.title: The PLR pathway and the afferent–efferent lesion map
units.guide: Afferent (I/L) limb: light on one eye → optic nerve; PLR fibres exit the optic tract before reaching the LGB to the pretectal nucleus (centre); PLR efferent neurons are primarily temporal. Efferent (B/L) limb: centre → internuncial neuron → B/L EWN (accessory nucleus for CN III) → B/L CN III → B/L ciliary ganglion → B/L short ciliary nerve → B/L sphincter pupillae constriction. ON, OC, OT are common to both the PLR and the visual pathway. Lesions of PLR: afferent — absolute/total (AAPO), relative (Marcus Gunn/RAPD), Wernicke's pupil; efferent — Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP), tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis.

units.title: Afferent pathway lesions — comparing AAPO and RAPD
units.guide: AAPO (complete optic nerve lesion d/t trauma, end stage optic nerve disease): light reflex test shows I/L DLR and C/L DLR absent when the lesion side is illuminated; symptom I/L anopia. RAPD (incomplete ON lesion d/t optic neuritis, CRAO, retinal detachment — ON is a collection of retinal ganglion cell axons): swinging flashlight test — on presentation B/L constricted, on stimulus B/L constrict on one eye, pupils dilate in the meantime on swinging, constrict again; repeat fatigues the lesioned ON → B/L dilation when the lesion eye is stimulated; no symptom. In both, pupils are always equal in size: isocoria.

units.title: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil and the Argyll Robertson pupil
units.guide: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil: I/L optic tract lesion → C/L homonymous hemianopia; light on the hemianopic/invisible VF gives no constriction, light on the normal VF constricts. ARP (efferent): causes — neurosiphilis (tertiary syphilis, may present with seizures/confusion), tabes dorsalis, aortic regurgitation; site — periaqueductal grey (affects I/L internuncial neurons) > posterior commissure (C/L internuncial neurons), usually B/L. Features: PLR B/L absent, accommodation/near reflex present (dorsal EWN carrying near reflex fibres is normal), no dilation with atropine, both pupils constricted on presentation (EWN receives neither excitatory/inhibitory signals). Mnemonic ARP PRA = Accommodation Reflex Present, Pupillary Reflex Absent.

units.title: Tonic pupil, pharmacological mydriasis and the anisocoria workup
units.guide: Tonic/Adie's pupil: ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve; causes — HZV ganglionitis, diabetes/alcoholism peripheral neuropathy, trauma; Holmes-Adie pupil = tonic pupil + ↓ deep tendon reflexes. I/L DLR ↓, CLR absent; near reflex present with slow vermiform dilating movements; denervation hypersensitivity constricts with 0.125% dilute pilocarpine (sphincter denervated → overexpression of receptors). Pharmacological mydriasis: drug action (e.g. atropine) supranuclear inhibition of EWN; does not dilate even with 1% pilocarpine. Anisocoria (difference ≥0.4 mm): greater in dark → abnormal pupil is constricted → 1% apraclonidine (positive = Horner's, negative = physiological); greater in light → abnormal pupil is dilated → 0.125% pilocarpine (constricts = tonic pupil; no constriction → 1% pilocarpine: constricts = 3rd CN palsy, neither = pharmacological mydriasis); abnormal shape = iris damage.
